You're probably going to disagree with this, but give it some thought.

First, I think you're right that what Canonical did with the Unity lens is bad and we shouldn't let them get away with it. However, bringing it up on threads like this is counter-productive. First because what the lens does is a pretty minor thing compared to the privacy disaster that is Windows and OS X. The lens doesn't enable mass surveillance the way proprietary software does, so as long as that's the only issue I think it's fine to ignore it when converting people to Linux. You can worry about raising their privacy and security standards after they made the switch.

Now the other reason I think this is not something to worry about is simply because Unity itself does a good job of turning off people from it. It is - and I don't think this just a matter of personal opinion - a pretty unattractive desktop. So if you don't want people using Unity, I would focus on that aspect of it.

There's a real cost to making people worry about this stuff before they even made the switch. It confuses them and shakes their trust to the point that it can make them give it up entirely.

That's a good point, but I always like to warn users before they get the idea that this is just how the entire Linux world is...

When you get a new user who has had zero Linux exposure, and they see that the flagship distro, which nearly everyone has suggested is slow, buggy, annoying, and collecting user data so that it can use their desktop as adspace... it could leave a bad taste in their mouth for Linux. But, if you warn them about these things "before they even made the switch," they will either avoid Unity altogether, or they'll know what Unity has in store before they gain the impression that Linux (as a whole) sucks.

You have to remember that, on top of developing an idea of what Linux "is," new users are also learning what a package manager is and how to use it (unless they're coming from an iDevice with Homebrew, which is a small percentage), developing a relationship with Terminal (which, again, most users have never had to do before), and learning a barrage of acronyms (GTK, QT, KDE, XFCE, GNOME, apt-get, pacman, yum, pkg, LXDE, ls, cd, pwd, etc), as well as all of the other things we just "take for granted." When they have all of this to face, they'll most likely just take the DE experience for granted, and assume that this is just how the DE works, and it'll be the same across all distros.

We know this isn't true, but new users won't necessarily know that...

Download drivers from NVIDIA. Exit Xwindows to the command prompt. Run the drivers, they are actually an executable binary. If you are missing dependencies, such as kernel headers (likely on a new install) you can use apt-get search "term" and then apt-get install <package name> to install them. Once the drivers are finished installing they will automatically fix up config files so you start using them upon restarting Xwin.

Do you need proprietary drivers? Nope. I prefer them, but other people prefer nouveau because its open source.

You probably don't need the proprietary drivers.

Installing the drivers with the installer from NVidia works, but is not recommended, as it may interfere with Debian's package system. The proprietary drivers are packaged for your convenience in the non-free repository. You may need to add " contrib non-free" to your sources list (probably in /etc/apt/sources.list) after "main", and update, then install nvidia-legacy-304xx-driver. Also install and run nvidia-xconfig.

If you compile your own kernel, you should compile it with make-kpkg, and use module-assistant to compile and install the appropriate nvidia modules.
